d: Share a controller, wheel, or HOTAS with the other PCs on your network. Both directions at once. Rumble, force feedback, adaptive triggers, lightbar, player LEDs, and speaker audio return to the real hardware. Pair once with a six-digit code. Works on your home network, and across the internet by swapping connection codes with no VPN needed.

Browse the community controller configs on the Steam Workshop and translate the one you pick into a PadForge profile: buttons, sticks, triggers, keyboard and mouse bindings, shift layers, and macros. Anonymous Steam connection, no account. An import report shows what came across clean and what was approximated. Off until you enable it in Settings.

Logitech, Fanatec, and Thrustmaster wheels driven in their own native protocols: constant force plus spring, damper, inertia, and friction. A Wheel tab for rotation range, auto-center, and RPM shift LEDs.

Route game rumble and force feedback to any audio output as low-frequency tones. Four voices with per-voice frequency (20–120 Hz) and gain, mono or controller-stereo split, and a frequency sweep to tune your shaker.
A virtual Switch Pro Controller through HIDMaestro, with gyro passed through from your physical pad. Games and emulators that speak Switch see the real thing.

One slot presents a SteamVR left and right hand pair, driven by any controller, keyboard, or motion source you map to it. Haptics return to the device you are holding. PadForge installs the SteamVR runtime itself, with no Steam account. Controls, not positional tracking, and one VR slot at a time.

Sony headphones with a head tracker become a motion source, confirmed on the WH-1000XM5 family. Turn your head to aim or lean, through the same gyro pipeline everything else uses. Found by capability rather than a model list. Rotation only, never position.

Play sound through the DualSense or DualShock 4 speaker. Mirror a Windows output or route a slot's macro sounds to the pad. DualSense over USB or Bluetooth, DualShock 4 over Bluetooth. Pads with haptic actuators but no speaker (Joy-Con, Switch Pro, Steam Controller, Steam Deck) play the sound as a haptic tone, and a Wii Remote through its own speaker.
Use a MIDI keyboard or pad controller as a mapping source. Notes, CC, pitch bend, and encoders bind like buttons and axes. Same Windows MIDI Services stack as the MIDI virtual output.
One row, any number of inputs, any number of devices. Six combine modes plus a drag-and-drop formula editor. Cross-device chords for free.
Caps Lock for your controller. Hold, Toggle, Latch, Cycle, Sticky, or No Button. Cycle steps a queue of layers with Next and Previous buttons. Per-layer color and emoji. Cross-device activators.

Browser-based gamepad over Wi-Fi. Ten controller layouts, a multi-touch touchpad, and a builder for your own. Up to 16 phones on one PC at once. Vibration API rumble back to each phone. No app install.
Pin a transparent touchpad window to any monitor and use it as a touchpad input for the assigned DS4 or DualSense slot. Adjustable opacity, size, and position. No phone required.

Map any touchpad (DualSense, DS4, laptop trackpad, phone web touchpad, overlay) to mouse X/Y with per-axis sensitivity and invert, to a virtual analog stick anchored where your finger lands, or to a wedge-thresholded D-pad. Plus the gesture stack: swipes, taps, longpress, pinch, rotate, custom shape templates. Every toggle is per slot.
Local, Player, and World reference frames. Real-world calibration. Cross-device Aim Engage. Tuning saves per pad per slot.

Two Mouse Position sources read where the desktop cursor sits and push a stick, trigger, or button toward it. A per-row Sensitivity dial (0.1 to 5.0) sets the cursor travel for full deflection. Separate from the Mouse Speed sources that read movement. Primary monitor only.

Native 2D art per profile, plus 3D models for Xbox 360, Xbox One / Elite / Adaptive, Xbox Series, DualShock 4, DualSense, DualSense Edge, and the Switch Pro pads. Click any button in 3D to record its mapping.
Scaled Radial, Radial, Axial, Hybrid, Sloped Scaled Axial, Sloped Axial. Per-axis anti-deadzone. Custom sensitivity curves with unlimited draggable points.
Full rumble passthrough. HID PID 1.0 for wheels and joysticks. Audio bass rumble synthesized from system audio. Constant force vector.
Seven DualSense trigger modes plus a one-click GameCube preset. Fourteen lightbar modes including audio-pulse, audio-band, Strobe, and Battery.
Xbox impulse trigger passthrough on the assigned physical pad. Same data routes to DualSense as Adaptive Trigger Vibration. Audio-bass trigger rumble.

Combo triggers and Custom Expression formulas. Key presses, mouse, scroll, volume, lightbar, rumble, and axis actions that latch, release, and scale. Twelve fire modes, from On Press through Double, Triple, Long, and Short Press to Toggle and Turbo, plus a per-macro shift-layer scope. Cursor actions to recenter the mouse, pin it at a point, or fence it inside a rectangle. Duplicate a macro in place, copy and paste between virtual controllers, or pull every macro from another in one step.
Watches the foreground window. Switches when a matching app takes focus. Win11-style flyout confirms.
Gyro and accel on UDP 26760. Cemu, Dolphin, Yuzu, Ryujinx all read it. Plug-and-play for any emulator that speaks Cemuhook.
Channel 1-16. CC for axes, Note On/Off for buttons. Real Windows MIDI Services endpoint. No loopMIDI bridge.
Sub-millisecond jitter via high-resolution waitable timers. Bit-perfect axis passthrough at defaults. Built on SDL3.
HidHide driver-level cloak. Per-device toggles auto-enable for gamepads. Cloak persists across launches.

In-app Bluetooth pairing. Press SYNC to bond once and reconnect on any button, or hold 1 and 2 for a temporary pairing. Wii Remote, Remote plus Nunchuk, Classic Controller, and Wii U Pro Controller map as pads. Accelerometer and Motion Plus gyro feed the motion pipeline. The IR camera drives an on-screen pointer, and a Balance Board reports weight and lean.

Read NFC tags through a PC/SC contactless reader and fire a macro on a tap. Register and name each tag from the Devices page. Every tag is its own trigger, next to an Any NFC Tag trigger. Media keys map too, and wireless pads show battery charge with an optional idle-disconnect timer.

Register a phrase and speak it to fire a macro. Recognition runs offline with no account and no cloud. The Vosk model downloads once on first use, and Windows' own recognizer carries the feature until it lands. Anything the recognizer hears that is not a registered phrase goes to an unknown bucket rather than firing at random.

Both PlayStation Move devices report over Bluetooth, and the PS4-era wand streams over USB as well. The wand carries a gyroscope, an accelerometer, an analog trigger and its illuminated sphere. The Navigation controller carries a stick, a D-pad and its buttons. Motion needs the wand's own calibration data, which PadForge reads once from a USB dock. There is no camera tracking, so you get rotation and acceleration but never position.
A headset's pose and its motion controllers become ordinary mapping sources, so what you hold in VR can drive a flat game.
The 6DoF puck reports as a six-axis controller: three translation axes and three rotation axes moving at once, plus its buttons. Games ignore the device class, so PadForge reads it directly.

A repeat action's rate follows how hard the input is pressed. Pick the analog source it tracks, a trigger or a DualShock 3 pressure axis, and a light press repeats slowly while a full press repeats at the interval.

Flick a stick or a touchpad and the cursor keeps traveling, coasting to a stop on constant-deceleration physics. Momentum Glide sets how far it coasts, and the touchpad adds fling controls for what a fast flick does.

A degree-ranged tilt mode beside the existing rate mode: hold a tilt and the stick holds its deflection, the way Steam's Joystick Deflection behaves. Full Tilt Range sets the angle that reaches full deflection, and Gyro Recenter re-zeroes the resting grip.
Get notified before a controller dies mid-game, at a percentage you set, with an optional buzz on the pad itself. The same rumble drives identify, which is how you tell several identical pads apart.
